statement: In randomized trials of people receiving chemotherapy (28 trials, 1,772 participants, mostly of nabilone, THC, levonantradol or dronabinol; 23 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo are associated with more people having complete control of nausea and vomiting: in a 2015 meta-analysis of the three placebo-controlled parallel-group trials that could be pooled (dronabinol or nabiximols; Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), 47% on cannabinoids against 20% on placebo had a complete response (the abstract's crude averages, their derivation not described; about 27 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42; 102 patients; I2 0%; low certainty by the review team). Twenty trials compared cannabinoids only with other anti-sickness medicines, most often prochlorperazine (15 trials), and these comparisons are not pooled in the article, so how cannabinoids compare with the anti-sickness medicines in use is not shown here. A narrative review calls THC an effective treatment for nausea and vomiting with chemotherapy and says patients often find marijuana more effective (Volkow et al., 2014; second-hand). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In three small trials (102 people having chemotherapy), about 47 in 100 people who took a cannabis medicine (dronabinol or a THC and CBD spray) had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 who took a dummy medicine (placebo). Most of the other trials compared cannabis medicines with other anti-sickness medicines, and this review did not combine them. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.
population: People receiving chemotherapy in randomized trials published up to April 2015
exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials (in the pooled placebo comparison, dronabinol or nabiximols; across all trials mostly nabilone, THC, levonantradol and dronabinol); doses are study conditions
comparator: Placebo (pooled); other anti-sickness medicines, mostly prochlorperazine (not pooled)
outcome: Complete response (complete control of nausea and vomiting as each trial defined it)
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, cannabinoid (dronabinol or nabiximols) against placebo, parallel-group trials, random effects: complete response 47% vs 20% (the abstract's crude averages; about 27 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42; 3 trials, 102 patients; I2 0%; GRADE low by the review team). Comparisons with active anti-sickness medicines (20 trials) not pooled in the article.

statement: In randomized trials of adults with chronic pain, mostly neuropathic or cancer pain (28 trials, 2,454 participants; 17 at high and 9 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines, mostly nabiximols (a THC and CBD spray used in the mouth), compared with placebo in trials with follow-up of at most 15 weeks, are associated with a small reduction in pain. In a 2015 meta-analysis of the parallel-group trials (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), 37% of people on cannabinoids and 31% on placebo had their pain reduced by at least 30% (the abstract's crude averages, their derivation not described; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), an odds ratio of 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 7 of them of nabiximols and 1 of smoked THC, 1,370 people; I2 48%) that does not exclude no difference, and pain on a 0 to 10 scale was 0.46 points lower with nabiximols (95% CI 0.11 to 0.80 lower; 6 trials, 948 people; I2 59%); the review team rated both moderate certainty and set no threshold for a clinically important change. The one smoked-THC trial gave the largest responder effect (OR 3.43, 1.03 to 11.48). More people rated themselves improved overall (OR 2.08, 1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 people; low certainty by the review team), neuropathic-pain scale scores were 3.89 points lower on a 0 to 100 scale (0.47 to 7.32 lower), and the Brief Pain Inventory (-0.17, -0.50 to 0.16) and quality of life (EQ-5D, -0.01, -0.05 to 0.02) did not differ. The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for chronic pain, but the outcomes so rated are either not statistically significant or small. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials of up to 15 weeks, people with long-lasting pain who took a cannabis medicine, mostly a THC and CBD mouth spray, scored their pain about half a point lower on a 0 to 10 scale than people who took a dummy medicine (placebo). About 37 in 100 people on the medicine and 31 in 100 on the dummy had their pain cut by at least 30%, a difference that could be due to chance. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.
population: Adults with chronic pain (mostly neuropathic pain; also cancer pain, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, HIV neuropathy and others) in randomized trials published up to April 2015
exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials: mostly nabiximols (oromucosal THC and CBD spray), also smoked THC, nabilone, THC spray, dronabinol, vaporized cannabis and others; doses are study conditions
outcome: At least 30% pain reduction; pain on 0 to 10 numerical rating scales; Brief Pain Inventory; Neuropathic Pain Scale; patients' global impression of change; quality of life (EQ-5D)
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, parallel-group trials, random effects, cannabinoid against placebo: at least 30% pain reduction 37% vs 31% (the abstract's crude averages; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 1,370 patients; I2 48%; GRADE moderate by the review team); smoked-THC trial OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48); neuropathic pain OR 1.38 (0.93 to 2.03; 6 trials); nabiximols: 0 to 10 pain scale WMD -0.46 (-0.80 to -0.11; 6 trials, 948 patients; I2 59%; moderate); Brief Pain Inventory -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16; 3 trials); Neuropathic Pain Scale -3.89 on 0 to 100 (-7.32 to -0.47; 5 trials); global impression of change OR 2.08 (1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 patients; I2 68%; low); EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02; 3 trials).

statement: In randomized trials of people with multiple sclerosis (11 trials, 2,138 participants; 3 further trials in paraplegia, 142 participants, could not be pooled; of all 14 trials, 7 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines, mostly nabiximols, compared with placebo in trials with follow-up of at most 15 weeks, are associated with a small improvement in spasticity as patients rate it, but not detectably as clinicians measure it. In a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), patients' own spasticity ratings on 0 to 10 scales were 0.76 points lower (95% CI 0.14 to 1.38 lower; 3 trials, 698 people; I2 73%; low certainty by the review team) and more patients rated themselves improved overall (OR 1.44, 1.07 to 1.94; 3 trials, 461 people; low), while the Ashworth scale, a clinician's rating of muscle tone, did not clearly change (-0.12, -0.24 to 0.01; 5 trials, 1,244 people; I2 0%; moderate; the corrected value), nor did the share of people whose rated spasticity fell by at least 30% (OR 1.64, 0.95 to 2.83) or 50% (1.40, 0.81 to 2.41; 2 trials each), activities of daily living (Barthel index, -0.58, -1.73 to 0.56; 4 trials) or walking speed (-0.86, -3.08 to 1.36; 2 trials). The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for spasticity, but the outcome rated moderate (Ashworth) showed no clear difference. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials of up to 15 weeks, people with MS who took a cannabis medicine, mostly a THC and CBD mouth spray, rated their muscle stiffness about three quarters of a point lower on a 0 to 10 scale than people who took a dummy medicine (placebo), and more of them felt better overall. When doctors measured stiffness, there was no clear difference. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.

outcome: Spasticity on the Ashworth scale (clinician-rated) and on patient-rated 0 to 10 scales; 30% and 50% reductions; patients' global impression of change; activities of daily living (Barthel index); walking speed
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, multiple sclerosis trials, random effects, against placebo: patient-rated spasticity (0 to 10) WMD -0.76 (95% CI -1.38 to -0.14; 3 trials, 698 patients; I2 73%; GRADE low by the review team); global impression of change OR 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94; 3 trials, 461 patients; low); Ashworth WMD -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01; 5 trials, 1,244 patients; I2 0%; moderate; corrected value, Table 2 still prints -0.11, -0.23 to 0.02); 30% reduction OR 1.64 (0.95 to 2.83) and 50% reduction OR 1.40 (0.81 to 2.41), 2 trials each (low); Barthel -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56; 4 trials; moderate); walking speed -0.86 (-3.08 to 1.36; 2 trials; moderate).

statement: For sleep problems, appetite and weight in HIV, anxiety, depression, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome, randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo or other treatments are too few, small or short to show whether they help: in a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), each of these conditions had one to four trials designed for it (four for appetite in HIV, at most two for each of the others) and none for depression, most of them small and many at high risk of bias. Sleep: in 19 placebo-controlled trials for chronic pain or multiple sclerosis, mainly of nabiximols, sleep-quality scores differed from placebo by -0.58 points (95% CI -0.87 to -0.29; 8 trials) and sleep-disturbance scores by -0.26 (-0.52 to 0.00; 3 trials), both very low certainty by the review team; of two trials in sleep problems (54 participants), one in sleep apnoea (22 patients; attributed to nabilone in the review, although its reference list points to a dronabinol trial) reported a lower apnoea–hypopnoea index (-19.64, P = .02), and a crossover trial in fibromyalgia found nabilone better than amitriptyline for insomnia (-3.25, -5.26 to -1.24); the review concludes, on low-quality evidence, that cannabinoids may improve sleep. Appetite in HIV: weight gain of 2 kg or more within 6 weeks with dronabinol against placebo, OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27; 1 trial, 88 patients), among 4 trials all at high risk of bias. Anxiety: one trial of cannabidiol in 24 people with social anxiety disorder, measured during a simulated public-speaking test with 107 minutes of follow-up (anxiety factor -16.52, P = .01; very low). Depression: in 5 trials for other conditions, 3 found no difference and one found worse depression scores at the highest nabiximols dose (2.50, 0.38 to 4.62) but not at the two lower doses (very low). Psychosis: two trials of cannabidiol (71 participants) found no difference, with intervals too wide to show the absence of an effect (against amisulpride, BPRS -0.10, -9.20 to 8.90; 35 patients). Glaucoma: one crossover trial of 6 people found no difference in eye pressure. Tourette syndrome: two small trials of THC capsules (36 participants) suggested less tic severity on some scales (17 or 18 patients per analysis; low). Epilepsy was not among the review's conditions; a narrative review describes only a parent survey of cannabidiol-rich cannabis in childhood epilepsy, in which 2 of 19 families reported freedom from seizures, and says safety and efficacy data were insufficient (Volkow et al., 2014; second-hand). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: For sleep problems, appetite in HIV, anxiety, depression, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome, there are only a few small, short trials of cannabis medicines each, so it is not known whether they help. Sleep scores in trials for pain or MS were slightly better with the medicine than with a dummy medicine (placebo), but this evidence is very weak. Epilepsy was not part of this review.
population: People with sleep problems, HIV/AIDS, social anxiety disorder, psychosis, glaucoma or Tourette syndrome in randomized trials published up to April 2015; sleep and depression scores in trials for chronic pain or multiple sclerosis
exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials: nabiximols, dronabinol, nabilone, THC capsules, cannabidiol, THC or cannabidiol spray; doses and timings are study conditions
comparator: Placebo; amitriptyline (insomnia), megestrol acetate (HIV) and amisulpride (psychosis) in single trials
outcome: Sleep quality and disturbance scores, apnoea–hypopnoea index and insomnia; weight gain; anxiety during a public-speaking test; depression scores; psychosis rating scales; eye pressure; tic severity
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015 (GRADE ratings by the review team): sleep quality WMD -0.58 (95% CI -0.87 to -0.29; 8 trials; very low) and sleep disturbance -0.26 (-0.52 to 0.00; 3 trials; very low) in trials for other conditions; sleep apnoea, apnoea–hypopnoea index -19.64 (P = .02; 22 patients; low); fibromyalgia insomnia, nabilone against amitriptyline -3.25 (-5.26 to -1.24), restfulness 0.48 (0.01 to 0.95); HIV weight gain of 2 kg or more, OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27; 1 trial, 88 patients; low); social anxiety, anxiety factor -16.52 (P = .01; 24 patients; very low); depression, highest nabiximols dose 2.50 (0.38 to 4.62), single-trial HADS 0.15, MADRS 1.90 and BDI 0.69 (all non-significant; very low); psychosis, cannabidiol against amisulpride BPRS -0.10 (-9.20 to 8.90) and PANSS 1 (-12.60 to 14.60; 35 patients; low); glaucoma, 1 crossover trial of 6, no difference; Tourette syndrome, single-trial differences on four tic scales with 17 or 18 patients (P = .03, P < .05, P = .061, P = .008; low).

statement: In randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines for many conditions (62 trials reported adverse events), cannabinoids at the highest dose each trial tested, compared with placebo or another medicine, increase short-term side effects: in a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), the odds of any adverse event were 3.03 times higher (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80; 29 studies, 3,714 patients; I2 31%), of a serious adverse event 1.41 times (1.04 to 1.92; 34 studies, 3,248 patients; I2 0%) and of leaving a trial because of adverse events 2.94 times (2.18 to 3.96; 23 studies, 2,755 patients), with no difference in deaths (1.01, 0.51 to 2.00; 5 studies, 929 patients). Specific effects more frequent with cannabinoids included disorientation (OR 5.41, 2.61 to 11.19), dizziness (5.09, 4.10 to 6.32; 41 studies), euphoria (4.08, 2.18 to 7.64), confusion (4.03, 2.05 to 7.97), drowsiness (3.68, 2.24 to 6.01), dry mouth (3.50, 2.58 to 4.75), somnolence (2.83, 2.05 to 3.91), loss of balance (2.62, 1.12 to 6.13), hallucination (2.19, 1.02 to 4.68; 10 studies), nausea (2.08, 1.63 to 2.65), asthenia (2.03, 1.35 to 3.06), fatigue (2.00, 1.54 to 2.62), vomiting (1.67, 1.13 to 2.47) and diarrhoea (1.65, 1.04 to 2.62); depression, anxiety, paranoia, psychosis and seizures did not differ clearly, with wide intervals (psychosis 1.09, 0.07 to 16.35; 2 studies, 37 patients). The review reports odds ratios only, not how many people in 100 had each effect; using the highest dose was the authors' choice of a worst case; and no study of long-term adverse events was found, even among non-randomized studies. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In short trials, people taking cannabis medicines had more side effects than people taking a dummy medicine (placebo) or another medicine: about three times the odds of any side effect and of stopping the trial because of side effects, and 1.4 times the odds of a serious one. Disorientation, dizziness, feeling high, confusion, drowsiness and dry mouth were among the most increased; nausea and vomiting were also more common. Deaths did not differ. The review used the highest dose each trial gave, did not say how many people in 100 had each side effect, and found no studies of long-term harms.
population: Patients with a range of conditions (chemotherapy, HIV/AIDS, chronic pain, spasticity, sleep problems, psychosis and others) in randomized trials published up to April 2015
exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials, at the highest dose each trial tested (mostly nabiximols, dronabinol and nabilone); doses are study conditions
comparator: Placebo or an active comparator medicine
outcome: Any, serious and treatment-stopping adverse events, deaths, and individual adverse events, in the short term
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, cannabinoid (highest dose) against placebo or active comparator, all indications: any adverse event OR 3.03 (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80; 29 studies, 3,714 patients; I2 31%); serious 1.41 (1.04 to 1.92; 34 studies, 3,248 patients; I2 0%); withdrawal due to adverse events 2.94 (2.18 to 3.96; 23 studies, 2,755 patients); death 1.01 (0.51 to 2.00; 5 studies, 929 patients); psychiatric disorders 3.10 (1.81 to 5.29; 8 studies); nervous system disorders 3.17 (2.20 to 4.58; 10 studies). Individual events: disorientation 5.41 (2.61 to 11.19); dizziness 5.09 (4.10 to 6.32); euphoria 4.08 (2.18 to 7.64); confusion 4.03 (2.05 to 7.97); drowsiness 3.68 (2.24 to 6.01); dry mouth 3.50 (2.58 to 4.75); somnolence 2.83 (2.05 to 3.91); loss of balance 2.62 (1.12 to 6.13); hallucination 2.19 (1.02 to 4.68); nausea 2.08 (1.63 to 2.65); asthenia 2.03 (1.35 to 3.06); fatigue 2.00 (1.54 to 2.62); vomiting 1.67 (1.13 to 2.47); diarrhoea 1.65 (1.04 to 2.62). Not significant: depression 1.32 (0.87 to 2.01), anxiety 1.98 (0.73 to 5.35), paranoia 2.05 (0.42 to 10.10), psychosis 1.09 (0.07 to 16.35), seizures 0.91 (0.05 to 15.66), dyspnoea 0.83 (0.26 to 2.63). No absolute frequencies.

statement: In studies of pregnant women and their newborns published from 1982 to 2014 (24 articles from 19 studies, mostly cohorts; 15 of the 24 articles before 2000, editors' count; English only), any cannabis use during pregnancy as each study defined it (women using other illicit drugs left out, but not those who smoked tobacco or drank alcohol), compared with no cannabis use during pregnancy, is associated with somewhat smaller babies and more admissions to intensive care, but not detectably with early birth. In a 2016 meta-analysis whose pooled estimates are crude, with no adjustment stated (Gunn et al., 2016; AMSTAR 2 critically low), exposed babies weighed on average about 109 g less at birth (95% CI 39 to 180 g; 10 studies, 4 of them finding lower weight; I2 63%), and had higher odds of weighing under 2,500 g (OR 1.77, 1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies, 2 of them positive; I2 89%) and of admission to neonatal or other intensive care (OR 2.02, 1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies, 3 positive; I2 78%), while preterm birth before 37 weeks (OR 1.29, 0.80 to 2.08; 9 studies), length of pregnancy, length and head size at birth, Apgar scores, birth defects and deaths around the time of birth showed no clear difference. No absolute risks were reported, and the review does not discuss whether intensive-care admission reflects the babies' health or hospital practice toward babies of mothers known to use drugs (editors' observation). Mothers who used cannabis also had higher odds of anaemia (OR 1.36, 1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies), a result carried mainly by one large study. The review's authors say that, because most studies did not separate cannabis from tobacco and alcohol, which themselves cause low birth weight and early birth, they cannot tell whether the associations come from cannabis. As described second-hand in narrative reviews and a professional statement: an earlier meta-analysis found that regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy reduced birth weight, though less than tobacco smoking did, and one large study found no rise in birth defects (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009); later large studies reported that the lower birth weight generally persisted after statistical control for other drug use, although cigarette smoking has often been hard to adjust for fully and self-reported use under-counts use (Hall, 2015); and in one US state with legal cannabis, prenatal use went with 1.5 times the odds of low birth weight after adjustment for maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use (OR 1.5, 1.1 to 2.1; Crume et al., as relayed by Page et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In studies mostly from before 2000, babies of women who used cannabis in pregnancy weighed on average about 109 grams less at birth than babies of women who did not, and more often went to newborn intensive care. Being born early, birth defects and deaths around birth were not clearly more common. Many of the mothers also smoked tobacco or drank alcohol, which also make babies smaller, and most studies did not separate these from cannabis, so the studies cannot show that cannabis caused the differences.
population: Pregnant women and their babies up to 6 weeks after birth, in 19 mostly cohort studies published from 1982 to 2014 in the USA, Canada, Australia, the Netherlands, Iran, Jamaica, Spain and Brazil; one later US state study as relayed by a professional statement
exposure: Any cannabis use during pregnancy as each study defined it (mostly self-report), with use of other illicit drugs excluded but tobacco and alcohol use allowed; frequency, amount, timing and potency not analysed
comparator: Women who did not use cannabis during pregnancy, and their babies (their tobacco and alcohol use not reported)
outcome: Birth weight; low birth weight (under 2,500 g); admission to neonatal or other intensive care; preterm birth (before 37 weeks); gestational age, length and head circumference; Apgar scores; birth defects and perinatal death; maternal anaemia
magnitude: Gunn et al. 2016 (pooled, no adjustment stated; random effects unless noted): birth weight about 109 g lower in exposed babies (printed as a positive mean difference, 109.42 g, 95% CI 38.72 to 180.12; 10 studies; I2 63%); low birth weight OR 1.77 (1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies; I2 89%); NICU or ICU admission OR 2.02 (1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies; I2 78%); preterm birth OR 1.29 (0.80 to 2.08; 9 studies; I2 85%); gestational age -0.20 weeks (-0.62 to 0.22; 5 studies; fixed effect); length -0.10 cm (-0.65 to 0.45; 6 studies; I2 59%); head circumference -0.31 cm (-0.74 to 0.13; 6 studies; I2 97%); maternal anaemia OR 1.36 (1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies; fixed effect). No absolute risks reported. As relayed by Page et al. 2020: one later US state study, low birth weight OR 1.5 (1.1 to 2.1) adjusted for maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use.

evidence.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Reproductive effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (begins p. 1385, continues p. 1386); Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 1389)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: high doses of cannabis cause growth retardation and malformations in animals, but epidemiological studies give scarce evidence of birth defects, and the few associations are hard to interpret because women who use cannabis in pregnancy are also more likely to use tobacco, alcohol and other illicit drugs, less likely to seek antenatal care and more poorly nourished; one large study saw no increased risk of birth defects. Reduced birthweight is the most consistent association in large epidemiological studies, and a meta-analysis found that regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy decreased birthweight, though less than tobacco smoking did, which the authors attribute probably to carbon monoxide. Conclusion: use in pregnancy could reduce birthweight but does not seem to cause birth defects.

evidence.locator: Reproductive effects of cannabis use › Fetal development and birth defects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (begins p. 3, continues p. 4)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: birth defects were not consistently increased, the most convincing null result coming from a large study that measured use by urinalysis; a meta-analysis of studies from the 1980s and 1990s found that regular use in pregnancy reduced birth weight, less than tobacco smoking did; several later large studies found reduced birth weight, an effect that has generally persisted after statistical control for other drug use, and some reported shorter labour and more babies small for gestational age. Limitations named: self-reported use is low and, by urinalysis studies, under-reported, which probably weakens the associations; and it has often been difficult to adjust fully for cigarette smoking.

risk_of_bias.note: Crude pooled estimates (no adjustment stated; continuous outcomes from raw means and SDs) in which tobacco and alcohol use, both known causes of low birth weight and early birth, are not separated from cannabis; exposure mostly self-reported and under-reported; AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_gunn_2016). A stricter reading would rate down two levels; the floor is reached either way.

inconsistency.note: Unexplained heterogeneity in the significant pools (I2 63% to 89%); most single studies found no association (6 of 10 for birth weight, 5 of 7 for low birth weight).

indirectness.note: Worded for the exposure as studied (any use, in articles mostly published before 2000); the second-hand reports only qualify.

imprecision.note: Wide intervals for low birth weight (1.04 to 3.01) and intensive-care admission (1.27 to 3.21); the preterm interval (0.80 to 2.08) fits both no difference and a doubling, so the absence of a link is not shown; pooled numbers of participants are not reported.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; not downgraded separately.

large_effect.note: The intensive-care odds ratio (2.02) is crude and confounded; no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Residual confounding by tobacco and alcohol would more plausibly inflate than hide the associations; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision: very low, the floor. Rated for the crude association as worded; these sources do not establish that cannabis causes the differences, and the review's authors say so. The narrative reviews and the professional statement are second-hand and overlap with the meta-analysis (Hayatbakhsh et al., 2012, is among its positive studies and among the later studies Hall, 2015, cites), so they qualify and are not counted as independent replication. Status mixed: the pooled estimates point to lower birth weight and more intensive-care admission, but most single studies found no association and the heterogeneity is unexplained.
